answer: An atlas is only as good as the surveys behind it, so a claim must be witnessed where it stands. Each identity needs two holders outside its own cluster to countersign its entry, and one countersignature backs one identity, so n aliases need n distinct witnesses instead of one crew. Every entry is priced by rank: the k-th filing costs k squared in bond, so a farm pays near n cubed while still needing unrelated guarantors. A lantern audit replays a random entry each epoch, and a ripple of failed replays voids the whole edition and forfeits its bonds.
